Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.23571.question: In the LLaMA/FineWeb experiments (Appendix E.5), what are BMuon’s dense validation loss and post-training MLP-channel pruning results versus Muon at matched training budget and pruning level? Report model size, seeds, training-time overhead, and any dense-quality tradeoff.

passages.text: NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

This section provides the experimental details and additional results for Section 5 . Appendix E.1 gives the ImageNet-1K post-training pruning setup and full pruning results. Appendix E.2 gives the CIFAR-100 post-training compression setup and full pruning results. Appendix E.3 studies the effect of the global budget K K . Appendix E.4 gives the gradual-pruning setup and architecture controls for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. Appendix E.5 provides the experimental details and full pruning results for the LLaMA/FineWeb experiments.

At evaluation, NuMuon compresses only the 12 MLP weight matrices using truncated SVD; attention weights remain dense. We distribute the retained rank budget as evenly as possible across matrices, with minimum rank 4. At each compression level, we choose the NuMuon rank so that the resulting whole-model parameter count is as close as possible to that of the corresponding structured-pruned model. Table 5 reports the exact post-training compression results corresponding to Fig. 2 . Table 5 : CIFAR-100 post-training compression results. Test accuracy (%) reported as mean ± \pm sample standard deviation over three seeds. All compression levels are evaluated independently from the final epoch-200 checkpoint, without post-compression fine-tuning.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

We evaluate gradual MLP-channel pruning during training from scratch on a ViT for CIFAR-100 and a ViT-S/16 for ImageNet-1K, targeting final pruning levels of 90 % 90\% and 95 % 95\% . All results are reported over three seeds. Each run starts dense and alternates between training and pruning. After each training phase, we rank all surviving MLP channels globally, permanently remove the lowest-ranked ones to reach the next sparsity target, and resume training from the surviving weights. We repeat this train–prune cycle until the final pruning level is reached, and then continue training for recovery. We compare three methods. Muon-mag trains with Muon and ranks channels by the coupled weight-magnitude score introduced in Section 5.1 . BMuon-mag trains the MLPs with BMuon ( α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 ) and uses the same magnitude ranking. BMuon- μ \mu uses the same BMuon training but ranks channels by the learned allocation μ \mu . During each BMuon training phase, the global budget is annealed to the next target channel count over the first half of the phase and held fixed for the second half. As an additional control, we test whether the architecture selected by BMuon- μ \mu is useful on its own. We keep only its final per-block widths, initialize a new model with those widths, and train it from scratch with standard Muon for the same training horizon. As a baseline, we also train a uniform-width model from scratch with nearly the same total number of MLP channels. Full details are given in Appendix E.4 .

The upper block reports the final pruned models after recovery; the lower block trains the architectures selected by BMuon- μ \mu from scratch with Muon and compares their accuracy with uniform-width models having nearly the same total number of MLP channels. The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

inspect:2610.11730.question: For the 124M–500M LLaMA experiments, how are spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched for validation loss, training budget, and SVD-LLM compression? What are the measured compression and inference-speed results, and what experimental controls or limitations qualify the comparison?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

inspect:2610.22794.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori's measured peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, throughput or step-time, and validation-loss results versus GaLore, other low-rank optimizers, and a full-rank baseline at matched rank and training budget? What costs does frequent subspace tracking add?

passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

Figure 1 : Trade-off between evaluation perplexity (Y-axis, lower is better) and peak optimizer state memory (X-axis, lower is better) for various low-rank optimizers in different ranks on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task. Bottom-left corner is the ideal region. Ori ( ⋆ \star ) forms a better Pareto frontier, achieving a superior performance-to-memory trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines like GaLore ( ∘ \circ ) and OSD ( □ \square ). However, existing adaptation strategies may overlook a key empirical observation that we make explicit in this work: the gradient subspace does not jump erratically but, rather, drifts smoothly after warm-up. In other words, the projector at step t t is predictably close to that at t − Δ ​ t t-\Delta t for small Δ ​ t \Delta t (e.g., 20). This slow, structured drift suggests a different perspective. Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

To demonstrate that the design principles behind Ori can be applied to specialized, state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers other than GaLore, we examine LDAdam [ 28 ] . LDAdam enhances the standard Adam optimizer by employing a projection-aware, momentum-based update alongside a generalized error-feedback mechanism. This design aligns with findings from MicroAdam [ 21 ] , which showed that applying error feedback at every iteration is essential for recovering Adam-like convergence at million- and billion-parameter scales (e.g., BERT/LLaMA). These techniques significantly enhance language model pre-training performance in extremely low-rank settings (e.g., rank 32 with an embedding size of 2048). However, LDAdam faces a critical barrier to practical deployment: it requires updating the projector at every training step ( T = 1 T=1 ) to maintain performance, incurring prohibitive computational costs. As shown in our later empirical results ( Table 2 ), when the update interval is increased to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule of GaLore – LDAdam’s performance degrades significantly. We attribute this drop to LDAdam’s reliance on a simple single-step power iteration method for subspace estimation, which we hypothesize is insufficient for tracking the drifting gradient subspace over large update intervals. Inspired by Ori, we introduce a multi-step stochastic power iteration mechanism into LDAdam’s update routine. We refer to this improved optimizer as O-LDAdam, reflecting its infusion of Ori’s online subspace tracking into LDAdam’s error-correcting framework. We provide further algorithmic details in Appendix D .

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . inspect:2610.22794.text:
A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

Figure 1 : Trade-off between evaluation perplexity (Y-axis, lower is better) and peak optimizer state memory (X-axis, lower is better) for various low-rank optimizers in different ranks on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task. Bottom-left corner is the ideal region. Ori ( ⋆ \star ) forms a better Pareto frontier, achieving a superior performance-to-memory trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines like GaLore ( ∘ \circ ) and OSD ( □ \square ). However, existing adaptation strategies may overlook a key empirical observation that we make explicit in this work: the gradient subspace does not jump erratically but, rather, drifts smoothly after warm-up. In other words, the projector at step t t is predictably close to that at t − Δ ​ t t-\Delta t for small Δ ​ t \Delta t (e.g., 20). This slow, structured drift suggests a different perspective. Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

To demonstrate that the design principles behind Ori can be applied to specialized, state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers other than GaLore, we examine LDAdam [ 28 ] . LDAdam enhances the standard Adam optimizer by employing a projection-aware, momentum-based update alongside a generalized error-feedback mechanism. This design aligns with findings from MicroAdam [ 21 ] , which showed that applying error feedback at every iteration is essential for recovering Adam-like convergence at million- and billion-parameter scales (e.g., BERT/LLaMA). These techniques significantly enhance language model pre-training performance in extremely low-rank settings (e.g., rank 32 with an embedding size of 2048). However, LDAdam faces a critical barrier to practical deployment: it requires updating the projector at every training step ( T = 1 T=1 ) to maintain performance, incurring prohibitive computational costs. As shown in our later empirical results ( Table 2 ), when the update interval is increased to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule of GaLore – LDAdam’s performance degrades significantly. We attribute this drop to LDAdam’s reliance on a simple single-step power iteration method for subspace estimation, which we hypothesize is insufficient for tracking the drifting gradient subspace over large update intervals. Inspired by Ori, we introduce a multi-step stochastic power iteration mechanism into LDAdam’s update routine. We refer to this improved optimizer as O-LDAdam, reflecting its infusion of Ori’s online subspace tracking into LDAdam’s error-correcting framework. We provide further algorithmic details in Appendix D .

Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions are required for the singular-mode results, and what experiments, if any, test whether the predicted low-rank bias of GD, Muon, SignGD, Shampoo, or K-FAC appears in neural-network or LLM weight matrices?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
passages.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 6: Singular mode trajectories reveal optimizer dependent spectral clocks. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. inspect:2610.10965.text:
The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

questions: In the NanoGPT speedruns, how does Spectrally Targeted Muon compare with standard Muon and normalized SGD on validation loss, training time or throughput, and the effective rank of weight matrices? What baselines, matched budgets, and limitations qualify the comparison?

inspect:2610.04507.question: In the 7B language-model label-noise experiment, what are the module-matched LoRA rank-sweep results versus dense fine-tuning for clean-test performance and noisy-label fitting? Report ranks, parameter counts, seeds, and whether the vision-model second-descent conclusion holds for the language model.

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

passages.text: Outside the window. At r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} , where either adapter can already express any dense weight update, both backbones remain behind dense. Under the shared rate, DeiT-Tiny passes a paired equivalence test with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a 0.05 0.05 -nat margin, a tenth of the cliff’s depth, first at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d (eight seeds), four times dense’s projection-weight count; ViT-Tiny does not pass it there. With each arm at its own best rate, dense gains from a higher rate while LoRA’s best at 3 ​ d 3d is the shared one, so the difference there becomes + 0.031 +0.031 nats, positive in every seed but inside the margin (Appendix C.2 ); the equivalence at 3 ​ d 3d is established only under the shared rate. The same shortfall at 7 7 B. To test the finding at language-model scale, we repeat the measurement on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) over 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% label noise, adapting the qkv projections of the last six blocks at twelve ranks up to d = 3584 d{=}3584 against dense fine-tuning of the same modules ( 3 3 shared seeds; Appendix C.3 ). Grouped-query attention makes the projections cheap relative to the adapter and places parity at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 , which we sample, so this axis is the clean test of the two references in Equation 1 . They part company sharply (Figure 3 ). At r = 448 r{=}448 the valley reference reads Rec = 1.06 \mathrm{Rec}{=}1.06 , a second descent that has already completed, while the dense reference puts the same point 0.058 0.058 nats short, and G G remains positive at every measured rank and in every seed, parity included. Read against a valley this sweep recovers fully; read against dense it never arrives.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

Models. passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

We compare against AdamW ( Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) , SOAP ( Vyas et al., 2024 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , and ALSO ( Romashov et al., 2026 ) . inspect:2611.17191.question: In the language-model rank sweeps, what validation perplexity and forgetting results does Rényi-2 effective-rank regularization achieve versus unpenalized LoRA at matched rank and training budget? Report model sizes, seeds, and any training-cost or quality tradeoffs.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

Concretely, we study regularized training objectives that augment the standard language-modeling loss L L with a capacity regularization term that focuses on maximizing the effective rank. Direct spectral differentiation requires care at rank-deficient updates and incurs SVD overhead (Appendix D .1). We therefore use an SVD-free surrogate, the Rényi-2 effective rank erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . We develop two approaches to increasing this effective-rank surrogate. First, norm-bounded capacity maximization couples a Roy–Vetterli lower bound with Norm-Bounded LoRA (NB-LoRA) Wang et al. (2025) : by enforcing an operator-norm cap and maximizing the Frobenius norm within that cap, one can raise effective rank through a principled constrained reparameterization. This strategy works in practice but limits the adapter weight updates to a specialized parameterization which often results in unstable training empirically. Therefore, we propose a simpler, differentiable, parameterization-agnostic and easy-to-optimize regularization strategy called the Rényi-2 penalty as our main method, which directly maximizes erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . This penalty is not only applicable to vanilla LoRA, but also to improved spectral variants such as PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) and LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2025) .

We first evaluate whether increasing adapter effective rank mitigates the learning–forgetting trade-off in a heterogeneous supervised fine-tuning setting that proxies continual learning. We report the Roy–Vetterli effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) of the accumulated update (higher indicates fuller use of available adapter capacity), training-mixture perplexity (Train PPL), and perplexity on the retention probes described above. This reported diagnostic differs from the Rényi-2 surrogate optimized by the penalty. Lower perplexity is better throughout. Figure 2 summarizes all methods across adapter capacity (panel A) and the learning–forgetting trade-off (panels B–D). The favorable region in the trade-off panels is the lower-left corner (strong learning with limited forgetting). Appendix Table 5 reports the full numbers; entries with ± \pm are means and sample standard deviations over three training executions, except PiSSA ( n = 2 n=2 ), and the remaining rows are single runs. PiSSA excludes one resumed execution with apparent data replay (Appendix G.1 ); its small two-run SD does not establish low population variability.

Figure 2: Dense FT denotes dense down-projection fine-tuning. Mixed-domain continual-learning baselines on Qwen2.5-0.5B (base, not Instruct; rank r = 896 r{=}896 unless noted). Each point represents a method–penalty configuration; the legend maps dot colors to adapter type. Points show multi-run means or single-run endpoints; sample SDs are reported in Appendix Table 5 . (A) Effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) shown as a vertical strip from 0 0 to nominal rank 896 896 (horizontal dashed line), with horizontal offsets only for visibility; higher indicates fuller adapter capacity utilization. (B–D) Learning–forgetting trade-offs: Train PPL (mixture learning) versus Wiki PPL, StarCoder PPL (pretraining proxies), and WMT CS–EN PPL (in-mixture translation retention); lower-left is better. The three Rényi-2 penalty points use different regularization weights λ \lambda . Unpenalized PiSSA and LoRA-XS have the highest Wiki perplexities; VeRA, SVF, and TinyLoRA limit forgetting with weaker mixture fit. NB-LoRA approaches the λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 learning–retention trade-off. Unpenalized PiSSA uses two runs after excluding one resumed execution with apparent data replay; the other multi-run points use three executions. Dense FT, LoRA at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , and penalized PiSSA at λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 are single runs. Full numeric values and the PiSSA exclusion are documented in Appendix Table 5 and its accompanying text.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

passages.text: LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. However, it often exhibits a performance gap compared to full fine-tuning. We here summarize several studies to improve the performance of LoRA. Modeling (Architecture). Beyond the standard two-factor factorization [ 21 , 41 , 36 , 24 ] as described in 2 , three-factor factorization has been proposed recently [ 58 , 26 , 41 ] , which inserts a small trainable matrix between B B and A A to fuse more information and flexibly. Other approaches have also been explored, such as adapting low-rank values at each module [ 66 ] , incorporating the mixture-of-experts architecture [ 15 , 32 , 16 , 50 ] , exploiting multiple LoRA modules [ 59 , 28 , 30 ] , and introducing non-linear mapping [ 13 ] . In this paper, we adopt the standard two-factor modeling 2 as a first step and leave the expansion for other advanced modelings to future work.

Initialization. Hu et al. [21] originally proposed to use a random Gaussian initialization for A A and set zero for B B to ensure that B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} is zero at the beginning of training. Later, several initialization strategies have proposed to utilize the pre-trained weight characteristics [ 33 , 54 ] . These methods differ in how they initialize B B and A A , using the largest singular values and corresponding vectors of the pre-trained weight matrix [ 33 ] or smaller ones [ 54 ] . On the other hand, Wang et al. [55] and Zhang et al. [67] initialized B B and A A using the singular values and corresponding vectors of the one-step gradient of full fine-tuning. In this paper, we follow the standard initialization proposed in [ 21 ] and the combination with the advanced initialization strategies is left for future work.

Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Others. To improve the performance of LoRA, several LoRA variants have been proposed. Hayou et al. [19] applied different learning rates to B B and A A and shows fast convergence. Liu et al. [29] decomposed the pre-trained weight into magnitude and direction, and then employed LoRA for directional updates to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Xia et al. [59] trained multiple LoRA sequentially like the residual learning to improve the performance of LoRA. Dettmers et al. [11] applied quantization to the pre-trained models with LoRA to save memory usage without sacrificing performance. We leave the combination of these studies with our method to future work.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . Figure 1: Training time comparison of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning.

Throughout this paper, we confirmed that our preconditioning improves the performance of LoRA. For further progress, we discuss the following future issues. (I) As a first step, we tested our preconditioning in the widely used SGD and AdamW optimizers. Extending our approach to other sophisticated optimizers is a promising direction for future research. (II) Our method is based on the standard two-factor factorization of LoRA. Combining other modeling, e.g., three-factor factorization [ 58 , 26 , 16 ] , with our method is left for future work. (III) Combining the state-of-the-art initialization strategies for LoRA with our method has excellent potential but is nontrivial because our approach may break those strategy concepts. We will explore this potential in the future. (IV) Our method is inspired by the first-order approximation of the weight update of full fine-tuning, which means each update is sufficiently small. We must consider the higher-order effective and will design more efficient preconditioning approaches in the future. (V) Testing our method on various models and tasks, e.g., image generation tasks for qualitative visual evaluation, is a promising direction for further assessing its practical utility.

inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search comparisons, what are CORE’s measured answer accuracy, evidence recall, and context-token or latency costs versus Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses across the three agent models and benchmarks? Were retrieval corpus, search budget, and agent model matched, and what limitations affect applying CORE to a handwritten research-digest harness?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Our CORE harness, illustrated in Figure 1 , manages tool execution and context construction for a language model agent performing deep research. The agent decides what information to seek, and the harness retrieves and presents the corresponding evidence. We consider a closed-search setting over a fixed collection 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Although this setting abstracts away the dynamics of the live web, it enables reproducible evaluation and controlled comparisons across agent models, retrieval backends, and harnesses. The agent follows a ReAct-style interaction loop ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Conditioned on the original question and the evidence accumulated in its context, the agent iteratively formulates sub-queries for the search interface and uses the returned evidence to guide subsequent searches or finalize the answer. Given the question x x , let I I denote the system instructions and tool descriptions. At turn t t , the agent operates as follows: C t \displaystyle C_{t} = [ I , x , y 0 , O 0 , … , y t − 1 , O t − 1 ] \displaystyle=[I,x,y_{0},O_{0},\ldots,y_{t-1},O_{t-1}] (1) y t \displaystyle y_{t} ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ C t ) \displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid C_{t}) (2) where C t C_{t} is the current context, y t y_{t} is the agent’s output at turn t t , and O t O_{t} is the resulting sequence of tool observations or harness feedback. Here, π θ \pi_{\theta} denotes the language model together with its decoding procedure. Each output either requests one or more tool calls or provides a final answer.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

Our experiments examine multi-step information seeking on three benchmarks with fixed text collections and reference answers. We chose this setting on purpose because it allows controlled, reproducible comparisons across harnesses. Fixed corpora do not capture the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of the open web, and reference-answer-based evaluation may not fully reflect the quality of long-form synthesis in less constrained research tasks. Evaluating on live web search and open-ended research reports is beyond the scope of this work. We leave it to future research, which could test whether our findings carry over beyond fixed-corpus question answering.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .
