Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

inspect:2610.20857.question: How was IDEA2PRIOR evaluated against ChatGPT and Gemini Deep Research for paper retrieval and ranking? Were queries, candidate access, evidence, and scoring comparable, what were the HARD-query results, and which components could transfer to a handwritten research-digest harness?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

inspect:2609.34264.question: In language-model fine-tuning, how does Rotated Manifold Optimization compare with standard LoRA and geometry-aware or matrix-optimizer baselines at matched adapter rank and training budget? Report held-out loss or task performance, convergence, step-time or memory overhead, model sizes, seeds, and limitations.

passages.text: Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We finetune Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , and Gemma-2-27B ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) at rank r = 16 r=16 on 100K MetaMathQA examples ( Yu et al., 2024 ) for one epoch, using an effective batch size of 128. We construct a held-out 10K-example validation set and measure validation loss as the mean cross-entropy over response tokens. For each optimizer, we independently select the learning rate that minimizes validation loss and repeat the selected configuration over three seeds. Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

inspect:2611.06598.question: In the LoRA fine-tuning experiments, how is behavioral rate measured, and what compressed adapter sizes and held-out performance are reported versus standard LoRA or other compression baselines? What model sizes, datasets, corruption controls, seeds, and limitations qualify the claim that correction spectra predict behavioral compressibility?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results

Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

passages.section: 5.2 Damage Is Structured Across Adapter Directions
passages.text: The effect is not restricted to a single model size or task. Additional experiments reproduce recovery across Qwen2.5 scales and other corrupted settings. On 72 off-task probes, the compressed corrupted adapter also remains closer to the frozen model than a clean fine-tune with comparable in-domain performance. Scaling, matched-norm, training-rank, cross-model, and off-task controls are reported in Appendix D . Together, these results show that compression need not merely degrade a fine-tuned update. When supervision induces both useful and harmful effects, those effects can be distributed very differently across the learned update, and aggressive bottlenecks can suppress them unequally. In the next section, we ask whether related properties of a successful update also predict how much rate is required to preserve its behavior.

The previous analysis asks what can be inferred before the update is trained. Once the learned update is available, a simpler relationship emerges. Section 5 showed that aggressive compression often acts behaviorally like shrinking the update, although it is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. This suggests that compression difficulty may depend on how far the learned update can be reduced before its acquired behavior is lost. Along this compression path, the realized rate is also approximately p p bits per original adapter value. Figure 7 (a) tests this correspondence directly. After fixing the rule on six adapters from two receivers, Figure 7 (b) compares this estimate with measured rates on 42 checkpoints from five other receivers. It achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value ( R 2 = 0.95 R^{2}=0.95 ). On a broader archive of 58 adapters spanning 34 corpora, the RMSE is 0.105 bits per value. Additional baselines, disjoint-evaluation controls, and trained-update predictors are reported in Appendix C.4 . These experiments remain retrospective: although the rule was fixed independently of the reported receiver panels, their behavioral rates had already been measured when it was formulated. We therefore interpret Equation 7 as a retrospective empirical approximation rather than a prospectively validated prediction law. The same response curve connects the two main empirical findings of the paper. In Section 5 , moving back along the learned update can remove harmful behavior and recover performance; here, the distance one can move before losing useful behavior closely tracks the rate required to preserve the fine-tune. Figure 7: Behavioral rate tracks update shrinkability. (a) Retained gain for three Llama-3.1-8B adapters when the uncompressed update is scaled by α \alpha (lines), together with compressed operating points placed at their effective scale p ​ γ p\gamma (dots). (b) α 90 / γ \alpha_{90}/\gamma against measured R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) for 42 checkpoints on five receivers not used to fix the rule (blue) and 58 archived adapters spanning 34 corpora (grey). No regression coefficient is fitted.

Our experiments show that behavioral rate is receiver-relative: the same dataset can require different rates across frozen models, while parameter-space reconstruction error alone does not predict which compressed updates preserve behavior. At the same time, the success of the shrinkability approximation indicates that, once an update has been learned, much of its compression difficulty can be summarized by the behavioral response obtained when moving back along that update. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, R ⋆ R^{\star} is an operational, codec-dependent rate rather than an information-theoretic optimum; different adapter parameterizations or codecs may induce different measured rates. Second, the correction-spectrum statistic is only a proxy for the full receiver-relative geometry and does not transfer reliably across receivers. Third, the shrinkability rule is supported by broad but retrospective evaluation, and remains to be validated prospectively on rates not observed when the rule is formulated. Finally, our recovery experiments use deliberately corrupted supervision to create a controlled mixture of useful and harmful effects. Whether the same structure governs naturally occurring fine-tuning errors remains an open question.

matches.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. matches.title: Convergence of Practical Muon with Finite Newton-Schulz Iterations and Nesterov Momentum
matches.abstract_excerpt: Practical Muon maintains momentum and performs a small, fixed number of Newton--Schulz iterations separately for each parameter matrix, often with a Nesterov correction. matches.title: Learn the Directions, Normalize the Gains: Post-Training Normalization for LoRA
matches.abstract_excerpt: While Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient task specialization, its learned updates can compromise capabilities beyond the target task. matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights

pending.reason: The inspected evidence supports ten strong, complementary matches. The material reviewer disagreement over RoM is resolved in its favor: matched-rank, multi-model fine-tuning results add practical evidence beyond the other LoRA-geometry papers. BMuon is omitted because its 1B language-model result trades substantially worse unpruned perplexity for structured-pruning robustness, rather than demonstrating low-rank compression at preserved quality. No unresolved uncertainty is likely to change this selection.

Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation $(B, A) \sim (BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for any invertible matrix $G$ because $BA^\top = BG^{-1}(AG^\top)^\top$ and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices $(BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for all $G$ are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix optimizers have emerged as a promising direction, with Muon standing out as a prominent design. candidates.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. candidates.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. candidates.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite

candidates.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduce

candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming $k$-PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3\% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontier

candidates.title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. candidates.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

candidates.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. candidates.title: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. candidates.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold $τ$, so that varying $τ$ interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix's isospectral manifold. candidates.title: Finite Spectral Depth Controls Gaussian Entrance Rank and Avoidance of the First Gradient-Flow Saddle
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton-Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton-Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four.

candidates.title: ReGRA: Residual-Gradient Adaptation for Complementary Low-Rank Fine-Tuning
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. candidates.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter's rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. 2610.23571:adb66ff3b22171daa692b42954851.question: Compared with standard Muon and other optimizer baselines, what measured compression and model-quality results does BMuon report for Transformers, especially the LLM experiment? Include pruning levels, accuracy or loss, training-compute cost, and experimental controls.

passages.text: NuMuon ( Dolatabadi et al., 2026 ) is the closest prior compression-aware variant of Muon. It imposes a nuclear-norm constraint on Muon’s update direction to improve low-rank compressibility. BMuon instead targets structured compressibility over hidden channels by introducing a global channel budget into Muon’s spectral-norm geometry. Prior work has also incorporated compressibility into training. Lu et al. (2022) train networks for unstructured pruning with Frank–Wolfe under fixed layerwise constraints on the weights, while Zimmer et al. (2025) use Frank–Wolfe under fixed norm constraints for convolutional filter pruning and low-rank compression. BMuon instead leaves the weights unconstrained and modifies Muon’s spectral update geometry for global hidden-channel compression. Resource-constrained structure learning and global structured pruning have been studied across CNNs and Transformers ( Gordon et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; An et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . GRASPrune ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns gates post hoc on a frozen LLM to select MLP channels and attention KV-head groups under a single global parameter budget, while DABP ( Laroui et al., 2026 ) jointly trains CNN weights and continuous channel gates under a global resource budget. BMuon uses no forward gates; its budget instead controls the channel-wise reweighting of Muon’s spectral update constraint during training.

Figure 2 shows the post-training fragility that motivates this work: Muon falls to 5.72 % 5.72\% test accuracy after only 30 % 30\% MLP-channel pruning. Muon+GL remains robust through 50 % 50\% pruning, while NuMuon degrades more gradually under low-rank compression. Under magnitude-based pruning, BMuon is substantially more compressible than the structured baselines while matching Muon’s dense accuracy: BMuon reaches 71.46 % 71.46\% , versus 71.49 % 71.49\% for Muon, 71.25 % 71.25\% for Muon+GL, and 69.95 % 69.95\% for NuMuon. Using μ \mu for ranking provides a further gain: at 80 % 80\% pruning, BM- μ \mu retains 70.57 % 70.57\% accuracy, compared with 60.84 % 60.84\% for BM-mag, while Muon, Muon+GL, and NuMuon have fallen to 1.93 % 1.93\% , 6.01 % 6.01\% , and 3.84 % 3.84\% , respectively. The advantage of BM-mag under the shared magnitude criterion isolates the compressibility benefit of BMuon training, while the further gain from BM- μ \mu indicates that the learned allocation also carries useful channel-importance information.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

Appendix E.2 gives the CIFAR-100 post-training compression setup and full pruning results. Appendix E.3 studies the effect of the global budget K K . Appendix E.4 gives the gradual-pruning setup and architecture controls for CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K. Appendix E.5 provides the experimental details and full pruning results for the LLaMA/FineWeb experiments.

We distribute the retained rank budget as evenly as possible across matrices, with minimum rank 4. At each compression level, we choose the NuMuon rank so that the resulting whole-model parameter count is as close as possible to that of the corresponding structured-pruned model. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

What are the measured compression and inference-speed results, and what experimental controls or limitations qualify the comparison?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

2610.22794:6cfd3007422c9c218e314cb91d4fc.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori's measured peak GPU memory, optimizer-state memory, throughput or step-time, and validation-loss results versus GaLore, other low-rank optimizers, and a full-rank baseline at matched rank and training budget? What costs does frequent subspace tracking add?

passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

Figure 1 : Trade-off between evaluation perplexity (Y-axis, lower is better) and peak optimizer state memory (X-axis, lower is better) for various low-rank optimizers in different ranks on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task. Bottom-left corner is the ideal region. Ori ( ⋆ \star ) forms a better Pareto frontier, achieving a superior performance-to-memory trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines like GaLore ( ∘ \circ ) and OSD ( □ \square ). However, existing adaptation strategies may overlook a key empirical observation that we make explicit in this work: the gradient subspace does not jump erratically but, rather, drifts smoothly after warm-up. In other words, the projector at step t t is predictably close to that at t − Δ ​ t t-\Delta t for small Δ ​ t \Delta t (e.g., 20). This slow, structured drift suggests a different perspective. Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

To demonstrate that the design principles behind Ori can be applied to specialized, state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers other than GaLore, we examine LDAdam [ 28 ] . LDAdam enhances the standard Adam optimizer by employing a projection-aware, momentum-based update alongside a generalized error-feedback mechanism. This design aligns with findings from MicroAdam [ 21 ] , which showed that applying error feedback at every iteration is essential for recovering Adam-like convergence at million- and billion-parameter scales (e.g., BERT/LLaMA). These techniques significantly enhance language model pre-training performance in extremely low-rank settings (e.g., rank 32 with an embedding size of 2048). However, LDAdam faces a critical barrier to practical deployment: it requires updating the projector at every training step ( T = 1 T=1 ) to maintain performance, incurring prohibitive computational costs. As shown in our later empirical results ( Table 2 ), when the update interval is increased to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule of GaLore – LDAdam’s performance degrades significantly. We attribute this drop to LDAdam’s reliance on a simple single-step power iteration method for subspace estimation, which we hypothesize is insufficient for tracking the drifting gradient subspace over large update intervals. Inspired by Ori, we introduce a multi-step stochastic power iteration mechanism into LDAdam’s update routine. We refer to this improved optimizer as O-LDAdam, reflecting its infusion of Ori’s online subspace tracking into LDAdam’s error-correcting framework. We provide further algorithmic details in Appendix D .

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

To demonstrate that the design principles behind Ori can be applied to specialized, state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers other than GaLore, we examine LDAdam [ 28 ] . LDAdam enhances the standard Adam optimizer by employing a projection-aware, momentum-based update alongside a generalized error-feedback mechanism. This design aligns with findings from MicroAdam [ 21 ] , which showed that applying error feedback at every iteration is essential for recovering Adam-like convergence at million- and billion-parameter scales (e.g., BERT/LLaMA). These techniques significantly enhance language model pre-training performance in extremely low-rank settings (e.g., rank 32 with an embedding size of 2048). However, LDAdam faces a critical barrier to practical deployment: it requires updating the projector at every training step ( T = 1 T=1 ) to maintain performance, incurring prohibitive computational costs. As shown in our later empirical results ( Table 2 ), when the update interval is increased to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule of GaLore – LDAdam’s performance degrades significantly. We attribute this drop to LDAdam’s reliance on a simple single-step power iteration method for subspace estimation, which we hypothesize is insufficient for tracking the drifting gradient subspace over large update intervals. Inspired by Ori, we introduce a multi-step stochastic power iteration mechanism into LDAdam’s update routine. We refer to this improved optimizer as O-LDAdam, reflecting its infusion of Ori’s online subspace tracking into LDAdam’s error-correcting framework. We provide further algorithmic details in Appendix D .

Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

passages.text: Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. We evaluate gradual MLP-channel pruning during training from scratch on a ViT for CIFAR-100 and a ViT-S/16 for ImageNet-1K, targeting final pruning levels of 90 % 90\% and 95 % 95\% . All results are reported over three seeds. Each run starts dense and alternates between training and pruning. After each training phase, we rank all surviving MLP channels globally, permanently remove the lowest-ranked ones to reach the next sparsity target, and resume training from the surviving weights. We repeat this train–prune cycle until the final pruning level is reached, and then continue training for recovery. We compare three methods. Muon-mag trains with Muon and ranks channels by the coupled weight-magnitude score introduced in Section 5.1 . BMuon-mag trains the MLPs with BMuon ( α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 ) and uses the same magnitude ranking. BMuon- μ \mu uses the same BMuon training but ranks channels by the learned allocation μ \mu . During each BMuon training phase, the global budget is annealed to the next target channel count over the first half of the phase and held fixed for the second half. As an additional control, we test whether the architecture selected by BMuon- μ \mu is useful on its own. We keep only its final per-block widths, initialize a new model with those widths, and train it from scratch with standard Muon for the same training horizon. As a baseline, we also train a uniform-width model from scratch with nearly the same total number of MLP channels. Full details are given in Appendix E.4 .

Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.
