2610.04249:404bd7a4ff40bc4d7b2bd7a3aae81.question: What balance and alignment assumptions are required for the singular-mode results, and what experiments, if any, test whether the predicted low-rank bias of GD, Muon, SignGD, Shampoo, or K-FAC appears in neural-network or LLM weight matrices?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Implicit bias of Adam and related adaptive methods.
passages.text: Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. (a) GD (b) Adam (c) Muon (d) Shampoo (e) K-FAC Figure 6: Singular mode trajectories reveal optimizer dependent spectral clocks. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Cattaneo et al. (2023) use backward error analysis to characterize corrections to Adam and RMSProp dynamics, relating implicit regularization to hyperparameters and training stage. The classification literature builds on the maximum margin characterization of GD for separable data ( Soudry et al., 2018 ) . Wang et al. (2021) study limiting parameter directions in homogeneous classification under their adaptive flow assumptions. Zhang et al. (2024) establish a maximum ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} margin result for full batch Adam in separable linear classification. Xie and Li (2024) connect AdamW, which includes decoupled weight decay, to ℓ ∞ \ell_{\infty} -norm constrained optimization under full-batch assumptions. Vasudeva et al. (2026) analyze a difference in feature learning between Adam and GD in a Gaussian classification model with two layer ReLU networks. These results concern distinct losses, optimizer conventions, or notions of bias. Our squared loss analysis studies finite singular amplitudes and phase times without weight decay, so classification margin results do not directly determine its birth or saturation laws.

Fig. 4 provides a broader validation of the theory in addition to the theoretical evaluation done in Sec. 6 . Fig. 5 compares the optimization and rank dynamics. Although the methods eventually reach similar losses and effective ranks, their trajectories differ substantially. GD learns the target modes sequentially and retains a low effective rank for longer, consistent with the small mode mobility factor σ p \sigma^{p} . Adam reduces this separation and activates weaker modes much earlier. Muon produces an even more rapid redistribution of spectral mass, reflecting its normalized spectral update. Cumulative Shampoo initially behaves more like GD but quickly changes regime as its accumulated preconditioner adapts. K-FAC exhibits a smoother evolution in which curvature correction reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales. The stable and effective rank curves therefore mainly differ during the transient phase, while their later agreement reflects the unique full observation target rather than identical optimization dynamics. Figure 5: Optimization and rank dynamics in matrix factorization. All optimizers train the same depth L = 4 L=4 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Left: training loss over optimization steps. Middle: stable rank of W W . Right: effective rank of W W . The optimizers exhibit markedly different transient rank dynamics despite converging toward similar final spectra. GD retains a lower rank representation for longer, whereas Adam, Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and K-FAC alter the rate at which spectral mass is distributed across modes.

The singular value trajectories in Fig. 6 make these differences more explicit. Under GD, larger target modes emerge first and weaker modes remain close to initialization for substantially longer times. This sequential emergence is the dynamical mechanism underlying its transient low rank bias. Adam substantially compresses these mode dependent delays, while Muon causes the positive modes to follow nearly the same spectral clock until they encounter their different target amplitudes. Cumulative Shampoo exhibits the predicted two stage behavior: early growth remains separated across modes, after which accumulated gradient history accelerates the weaker modes and reduces target amplitude dependence. K-FAC produces the weakest separation between mode trajectories, consistent with curvature correction compensating for the factorization induced mobility barrier. These trajectories illustrate that optimizers reaching similar final solutions can nevertheless pass through very different spectral representations during training. GD exhibits strongly sequential learning;Adam reduces these delays, while Muon makes the modes evolve on nearly the same clock until they approach their respective targets. Cumulative Shampoo shows a faster history adapted growth of weaker modes. K-FAC further reduces the factorization induced separation between mode time scales through curvature correction. The common final amplitudes are determined by the unique full observation target, whereas the transient trajectories expose the distinct inductive biases of the optimizers.

2610.10965:ec80e7a9c3aa3bc38967809f9d14c.question: In the NanoGPT speedruns, how does Spectrally Targeted Muon compare with standard Muon and normalized SGD on validation loss, training time or throughput, and the effective rank of weight matrices? What baselines, matched budgets, and limitations qualify the comparison?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

Figure 3 (a) shows that the singular values are spread across many orders of magnitude, indicating that gradient matrices in the language model setting are very poorly conditioned. This variation does not stem from variation between different matrices: as we can see in Figure 4 (a), the effective rank of the gradient stays below about 280 for most of training. This implies a low-entropy and highly nonuniform distribution within each matrix. Figure 3 (a) also displays the distribution of the gradients after Nesterov momentum is applied. Momentum thins out the low end of the spectrum, suggesting that it suppresses some noisy directions, but otherwise leaves its shape alone and simply shifts scale. This distribution was used to select the absolute thresholds τ \tau for targeted Muon. Averaged over matrices, the top arm lifts about 1% to 28% of the singular directions, and the bottom arm lifts from nearly all of the directions down to about 30%. In terms of squared Frobenius norm, the lifted band holds 32–96% of the momentum in the top arm and at most 13% in the bottom arm. Note that τ \tau is absolute while the bulk of the spectrum sits at different levels in different matrices, so the same τ \tau lifts very different fractions of different matrices. In the top arm this compounds: a matrix whose spectrum falls below τ \tau only gets its raw momentum and effectively stops training, so at the larger thresholds most of the deeper layers are left untouched. Also note that every momentum singular value is far below one, so the targeted region is always amplified, not suppressed.

still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. This suggests that keeping the spectrum flat is cheap, but isn’t what drives performance.

Our work also suggests an explanation as to why warmup costs Muon but helps AdamW, using the structural plots. AdamW is slow to build structure: its zero-initialized output projections take the whole run to build rank and are still rising at the end (Figure 4 (d)), its early updates lie almost entirely in the parameters’ own frame (Figure 5 (a)), and its gradients have the lowest effective rank of any optimizer over the first hundred steps, lower than any Muon variant that builds structure at all. An elementwise normalized update builds a matrix one bounded increment at a time, so how well it builds depends on how big the first steps are, and with warmup AdamW ends with higher parameter rank and lower loss. An orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step, so Muon’s structure is the same with or without warmup and warmup only throws away full-rate steps.

2610.04507:240a1e628a4ee38d547be62ce0bc7.question: In the 7B language-model label-noise experiment, what are the module-matched LoRA rank-sweep results versus dense fine-tuning for clean-test performance and noisy-label fitting? Report ranks, parameter counts, seeds, and whether the vision-model second-descent conclusion holds for the language model.

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

passages.section: 5.3 The parameter-saving window closes before the descent arrives
passages.text: Outside the window. At r expr r_{\mathrm{expr}} , where either adapter can already express any dense weight update, both backbones remain behind dense. Under the shared rate, DeiT-Tiny passes a paired equivalence test with two one-sided tests (TOST) against a 0.05 0.05 -nat margin, a tenth of the cliff’s depth, first at r = 3 ​ d r{=}3d (eight seeds), four times dense’s projection-weight count; ViT-Tiny does not pass it there. With each arm at its own best rate, dense gains from a higher rate while LoRA’s best at 3 ​ d 3d is the shared one, so the difference there becomes + 0.031 +0.031 nats, positive in every seed but inside the margin (Appendix C.2 ); the equivalence at 3 ​ d 3d is established only under the shared rate. The same shortfall at 7 7 B. To test the finding at language-model scale, we repeat the measurement on Qwen2.5-7B ( Qwen Team, 2024 ) over 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples ( Zhang et al., 2015 ) with 20 % 20\% label noise, adapting the qkv projections of the last six blocks at twelve ranks up to d = 3584 d{=}3584 against dense fine-tuning of the same modules ( 3 3 shared seeds; Appendix C.3 ). Grouped-query attention makes the projections cheap relative to the adapter and places parity at r ≈ 1075 r{\approx}1075 , which we sample, so this axis is the clean test of the two references in Equation 1 . They part company sharply (Figure 3 ). At r = 448 r{=}448 the valley reference reads Rec = 1.06 \mathrm{Rec}{=}1.06 , a second descent that has already completed, while the dense reference puts the same point 0.058 0.058 nats short, and G G remains positive at every measured rank and in every seed, parity included. Read against a valley this sweep recovers fully; read against dense it never arrives.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

Data. CIFAR-100/CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) images are upsampled bilinearly to 224 2 224^{2} and normalized with ImageNet statistics (ViT-Tiny uses the 0.5 0.5 normalization of its checkpoint). Subsets are class-balanced ( n / C n/C per class over C C classes, selected by seed-controlled RNG). Symmetric label noise resamples a fraction η \eta of training labels uniformly among the remaining C − 1 C-1 classes; the noise pattern is seed-controlled and identical across ranks within a seed. No data augmentation is used in the main sweeps (isolating the capacity axis); E23 repeats the noisy rank sweep with random flip, pad-and-crop ( 16 16 px at 224 2 224^{2} scale, one offset shared per batch), and mixup ( α = 0.2 \alpha{=}0.2 ). Models. We use DeiT-Tiny ( 5.7 5.7 M parameters, patch 16 16 , width 192 192 ) and DeiT-Small ( Touvron et al., 2021 ) from timm ( Wightman, 2019 ) with ImageNet-1k pretrained weights; the classification head is replaced by a freshly initialized linear layer. ViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny are described in Table 14 , and Qwen2.5-7B in Appendix C.3 . LoRA wraps the fused qkv linear layers of the last six blocks; A A is initialized with Kaiming-uniform values and B B with zeros, so training starts at the pretrained function. The scaling schemes are fixed ( s = 1 s=1 ), standard ( s = α / r s=\alpha/r , α = 16 \alpha=16 ), and rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 , s = α / r s=\alpha/\sqrt{r} , α = 16 \alpha=16 ;) . In E15, LoRA adapts the fused c_attn projection of the last six blocks of GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) ; training runs for 12 12 epochs at lr 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} on 5,000 5{,}000 AG News examples with 20 % 20\% label noise, and there is no dense arm.

Training. We train with AdamW (lr 5 × 10 − 4 5\times 10^{-4} unless swept, wd 10 − 2 10^{-2} , cosine annealing to 0 0 , batch 64 64 ) and bfloat16 autocast for 40 40 epochs unless stated. Each run logs train/test NLL and accuracy every 5 5 epochs, final per-example test logits, and per-layer stable ranks of the update. Calibration protocol. Temperature is fit by grid/LBFGS on a class-balanced 5 5 k split drawn from the training pool, disjoint from the training subset, with true labels (clean); test labels are never used for fitting. passages.text: Training large language models (LLMs) entails a fundamental trade-off: memory-efficient optimizers such as Adam discard cross-parameter curvature, whereas full-curvature methods such as SOAP can accelerate convergence at prohibitive memory costs. We introduce Clean , a memory-efficient and full-curvature optimizer designed to resolve this bottleneck. Clean leverages the randomized Nyström method to accurately approximate the left and right preconditioners in SOAP, and to reduce the optimizer’s memory complexity from quadratic to linear in terms of model dimensions. We subsequently reintegrate the off-subspace components to capture curvature information beyond the low-rank approximation, preserving rich curvature at minimal memory cost. We further propose Q-Clean , a low-precision variant that aggressively compresses optimizer states. Q-Clean reduces optimizer memory consumption by over 50% compared to Muon when pre-training a LLaMA-1.3B architecture, all while maintaining strong and competitive predictive performance. Notably, Clean operates with a smaller optimizer-state footprint than standard AdamW while reaching AdamW’s final performance 26% faster in wall-clock time. Furthermore, our methods uniquely enable the pre-training of a 13B-parameter model on a single 80GB GPU, providing a scalable, efficient, and accessible approach to large-scale model optimization. $*$ $*$ footnotetext: Equal contribution.

2611.17191:4b17e89452a9adb282ac6df9e8129.question: In the language-model rank sweeps, what validation perplexity and forgetting results does Rényi-2 effective-rank regularization achieve versus unpenalized LoRA at matched rank and training budget? Report model sizes, seeds, and any training-cost or quality tradeoffs.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

ning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at https://github.com/tomohiro-sawada/lora-capacity-utilization .

Concretely, we study regularized training objectives that augment the standard language-modeling loss L L with a capacity regularization term that focuses on maximizing the effective rank. Direct spectral differentiation requires care at rank-deficient updates and incurs SVD overhead (Appendix D .1). We therefore use an SVD-free surrogate, the Rényi-2 effective rank erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . We develop two approaches to increasing this effective-rank surrogate. First, norm-bounded capacity maximization couples a Roy–Vetterli lower bound with Norm-Bounded LoRA (NB-LoRA) Wang et al. (2025) : by enforcing an operator-norm cap and maximizing the Frobenius norm within that cap, one can raise effective rank through a principled constrained reparameterization. This strategy works in practice but limits the adapter weight updates to a specialized parameterization which often results in unstable training empirically. Therefore, we propose a simpler, differentiable, parameterization-agnostic and easy-to-optimize regularization strategy called the Rényi-2 penalty as our main method, which directly maximizes erank 2 ​ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}_{2}(\Delta W) . This penalty is not only applicable to vanilla LoRA, but also to improved spectral variants such as PiSSA Meng et al. (2025) and LoRA-XS Bałazy et al. (2025) .

We first evaluate whether increasing adapter effective rank mitigates the learning–forgetting trade-off in a heterogeneous supervised fine-tuning setting that proxies continual learning. We report the Roy–Vetterli effective rank erank ⁡ ( Δ ​ W ) \mathrm{erank}(\Delta W) of the accumulated update (higher indicates fuller use of available adapter capacity), training-mixture perplexity (Train PPL), and perplexity on the retention probes described above. This reported diagnostic differs from the Rényi-2 surrogate optimized by the penalty. Lower perplexity is better throughout. Figure 2 summarizes all methods across adapter capacity (panel A) and the learning–forgetting trade-off (panels B–D). The favorable region in the trade-off panels is the lower-left corner (strong learning with limited forgetting). Appendix Table 5 reports the full numbers; entries with ± \pm are means and sample standard deviations over three training executions, except PiSSA ( n = 2 n=2 ), and the remaining rows are single runs. PiSSA excludes one resumed execution with apparent data replay (Appendix G.1 ); its small two-run SD does not establish low population variability.

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

2610.08049:9eeb7148f079af2f3b7f24e0de2a9.question: In language-model fine-tuning, how does the proposed Riemannian LoRA preconditioner compare with standard LoRA and other geometry-aware baselines at matched adapter rank and training budget? passages.text: LoRA was initially formulated by Hu et al. [21] and achieves comparable full fine-tuning performance despite having very few trainable parameters. However, it often exhibits a performance gap compared to full fine-tuning. We here summarize several studies to improve the performance of LoRA. Modeling (Architecture). Beyond the standard two-factor factorization [ 21 , 41 , 36 , 24 ] as described in 2 , three-factor factorization has been proposed recently [ 58 , 26 , 41 ] , which inserts a small trainable matrix between B B and A A to fuse more information and flexibly. Other approaches have also been explored, such as adapting low-rank values at each module [ 66 ] , incorporating the mixture-of-experts architecture [ 15 , 32 , 16 , 50 ] , exploiting multiple LoRA modules [ 59 , 28 , 30 ] , and introducing non-linear mapping [ 13 ] . In this paper, we adopt the standard two-factor modeling 2 as a first step and leave the expansion for other advanced modelings to future work.

Initialization. Hu et al. [21] originally proposed to use a random Gaussian initialization for A A and set zero for B B to ensure that B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} is zero at the beginning of training. Later, several initialization strategies have proposed to utilize the pre-trained weight characteristics [ 33 , 54 ] . These methods differ in how they initialize B B and A A , using the largest singular values and corresponding vectors of the pre-trained weight matrix [ 33 ] or smaller ones [ 54 ] . On the other hand, Wang et al. [55] and Zhang et al. [67] initialized B B and A A using the singular values and corresponding vectors of the one-step gradient of full fine-tuning. In this paper, we follow the standard initialization proposed in [ 21 ] and the combination with the advanced initialization strategies is left for future work.

Optimization. Several optimization approaches for LoRA have been proposed [ 56 , 69 , 26 , 41 ] . For example, Wang et al. [56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Others. To improve the performance of LoRA, several LoRA variants have been proposed. Hayou et al. [19] applied different learning rates to B B and A A and shows fast convergence. Liu et al. [29] decomposed the pre-trained weight into magnitude and direction, and then employed LoRA for directional updates to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Xia et al. [59] trained multiple LoRA sequentially like the residual learning to improve the performance of LoRA. Dettmers et al. [11] applied quantization to the pre-trained models with LoRA to save memory usage without sacrificing performance. We leave the combination of these studies with our method to future work.

To validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically, we investigate how preconditioning affects training time. For this purpose, we compared training times of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning. The experimental setup was the same as that described in Sec. 7.3 . The difference in training times mainly stems from dataset size and the computational cost of preconditioning. Figure 1 shows the results. Each method shows the mean and standard deviation of training times over all learning rates we used for validation. We observed that, although there are some differences due to constant time factors, the results are almost the same across all methods, including the AdamW with our preconditioning 5 as it admits the efficient implementation described in Sec. 5.1 . Consequently, these results validate the time complexity analysis in Sec. 5.1 empirically and show the computational efficiency of our preconditioning 5 . Figure 1: Training time comparison of the CLIP ViT-B/32 model on the seven image classification datasets when using the AdamW methods with different preconditioning.

Throughout this paper, we confirmed that our preconditioning improves the performance of LoRA. For further progress, we discuss the following future issues. (I) As a first step, we tested our preconditioning in the widely used SGD and AdamW optimizers. Extending our approach to other sophisticated optimizers is a promising direction for future research. (II) Our method is based on the standard two-factor factorization of LoRA. Combining other modeling, e.g., three-factor factorization [ 58 , 26 , 16 ] , with our method is left for future work. (III) Combining the state-of-the-art initialization strategies for LoRA with our method has excellent potential but is nontrivial because our approach may break those strategy concepts. We will explore this potential in the future. (IV) Our method is inspired by the first-order approximation of the weight update of full fine-tuning, which means each update is sufficiently small. We must consider the higher-order effective and will design more efficient preconditioning approaches in the future. (V) Testing our method on various models and tasks, e.g., image generation tasks for qualitative visual evaluation, is a promising direction for further assessing its practical utility.

2611.07859:0632de4fe95f281bb7b536e3695f3.question: In the controlled closed-search comparisons, what are CORE’s measured answer accuracy, evidence recall, and context-token or latency costs versus Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses across the three agent models and benchmarks? Were retrieval corpus, search budget, and agent model matched, and what limitations affect applying CORE to a handwritten research-digest harness?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Our CORE harness, illustrated in Figure 1 , manages tool execution and context construction for a language model agent performing deep research. The agent decides what information to seek, and the harness retrieves and presents the corresponding evidence. We consider a closed-search setting over a fixed collection 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Although this setting abstracts away the dynamics of the live web, it enables reproducible evaluation and controlled comparisons across agent models, retrieval backends, and harnesses. The agent follows a ReAct-style interaction loop ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Conditioned on the original question and the evidence accumulated in its context, the agent iteratively formulates sub-queries for the search interface and uses the returned evidence to guide subsequent searches or finalize the answer. Given the question x x , let I I denote the system instructions and tool descriptions. At turn t t , the agent operates as follows: C t \displaystyle C_{t} = [ I , x , y 0 , O 0 , … , y t − 1 , O t − 1 ] \displaystyle=[I,x,y_{0},O_{0},\ldots,y_{t-1},O_{t-1}] (1) y t \displaystyle y_{t} ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ C t ) \displaystyle\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid C_{t}) (2) where C t C_{t} is the current context, y t y_{t} is the agent’s output at turn t t , and O t O_{t} is the resulting sequence of tool observations or harness feedback. Here, π θ \pi_{\theta} denotes the language model together with its decoding procedure. Each output either requests one or more tool calls or provides a final answer.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

Our experiments examine multi-step information seeking on three benchmarks with fixed text collections and reference answers. We chose this setting on purpose because it allows controlled, reproducible comparisons across harnesses. Fixed corpora do not capture the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of the open web, and reference-answer-based evaluation may not fully reflect the quality of long-form synthesis in less constrained research tasks. Evaluating on live web search and open-ended research reports is beyond the scope of this work. We leave it to future research, which could test whether our findings carry over beyond fixed-corpus question answering.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

2609.34264:c6f1d1889f79116bf7bcab230de96.question: In language-model fine-tuning, how does Rotated Manifold Optimization compare with standard LoRA and geometry-aware or matrix-optimizer baselines at matched adapter rank and training budget? Report held-out loss or task performance, convergence, step-time or memory overhead, model sizes, seeds, and limitations.

passages.text: Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We finetune Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , and Gemma-2-27B ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) at rank r = 16 r=16 on 100K MetaMathQA examples ( Yu et al., 2024 ) for one epoch, using an effective batch size of 128. We construct a held-out 10K-example validation set and measure validation loss as the mean cross-entropy over response tokens. For each optimizer, we independently select the learning rate that minimizes validation loss and repeat the selected configuration over three seeds. Training for additional epochs did not further reduce the final validation loss. We evaluate downstream performance using zero-shot accuracy on GSM8K (1319 examples) and MATH (5000 examples) with greedy decoding and bfloat16 precision. Figure 1 shows the validation-loss trajectories for the two Llama models. Tables 1 and 2 report the mean and standard deviation of the final validation loss and downstream accuracies for the Llama models and Gemma-2-27B, respectively. 2611.06598:829dc79e1ef97b454074d6a20b74f.question: In the LoRA fine-tuning experiments, how is behavioral rate measured, and what compressed adapter sizes and held-out performance are reported versus standard LoRA or other compression baselines? What model sizes, datasets, corruption controls, seeds, and limitations qualify the claim that correction spectra predict behavioral compressibility?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results

Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

passages.section: 5.2 Damage Is Structured Across Adapter Directions
passages.text: The effect is not restricted to a single model size or task. Additional experiments reproduce recovery across Qwen2.5 scales and other corrupted settings. On 72 off-task probes, the compressed corrupted adapter also remains closer to the frozen model than a clean fine-tune with comparable in-domain performance. Scaling, matched-norm, training-rank, cross-model, and off-task controls are reported in Appendix D . Together, these results show that compression need not merely degrade a fine-tuned update. When supervision induces both useful and harmful effects, those effects can be distributed very differently across the learned update, and aggressive bottlenecks can suppress them unequally. In the next section, we ask whether related properties of a successful update also predict how much rate is required to preserve its behavior.

The previous analysis asks what can be inferred before the update is trained. Once the learned update is available, a simpler relationship emerges. Section 5 showed that aggressive compression often acts behaviorally like shrinking the update, although it is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. This suggests that compression difficulty may depend on how far the learned update can be reduced before its acquired behavior is lost. Estimating α 90 \alpha_{90} requires evaluating only five scales of the uncompressed update on 64 held-out examples, while γ \gamma is obtained from the adapter weights; no regression coefficient is fitted. After fixing the rule on six adapters from two receivers, Figure 7 (b) compares this estimate with measured rates on 42 checkpoints from five other receivers. It achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value ( R 2 = 0.95 R^{2}=0.95 ). On a broader archive of 58 adapters spanning 34 corpora, the RMSE is 0.105 bits per value. Additional baselines, disjoint-evaluation controls, and trained-update predictors are reported in Appendix C.4 . These experiments remain retrospective: although the rule was fixed independently of the reported receiver panels, their behavioral rates had already been measured when it was formulated. We therefore interpret Equation 7 as a retrospective empirical approximation rather than a prospectively validated prediction law. The same response curve connects the two main empirical findings of the paper. In Section 5 , moving back along the learned update can remove harmful behavior and recover performance; here, the distance one can move before losing useful behavior closely tracks the rate required to preserve the fine-tune. Figure 7: Behavioral rate tracks update shrinkability. (a) Retained gain for three Llama-3.1-8B adapters when the uncompressed update is scaled by α \alpha (lines), together with compressed operating points placed at their effective scale p ​ γ p\gamma (dots). (b) α 90 / γ \alpha_{90}/\gamma against measured R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) for 42 checkpoints on five receivers not used to fix the rule (blue) and 58 archived adapters spanning 34 corpora (grey). No regression coefficient is fitted.

Our experiments show that behavioral rate is receiver-relative: the same dataset can require different rates across frozen models, while parameter-space reconstruction error alone does not predict which compressed updates preserve behavior. At the same time, the success of the shrinkability approximation indicates that, once an update has been learned, much of its compression difficulty can be summarized by the behavioral response obtained when moving back along that update. Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, R ⋆ R^{\star} is an operational, codec-dependent rate rather than an information-theoretic optimum; different adapter parameterizations or codecs may induce different measured rates. Second, the correction-spectrum statistic is only a proxy for the full receiver-relative geometry and does not transfer reliably across receivers. Third, the shrinkability rule is supported by broad but retrospective evaluation, and remains to be validated prospectively on rates not observed when the rule is formulated. Finally, our recovery experiments use deliberately corrupted supervision to create a controlled mixture of useful and harmful effects. Whether the same structure governs naturally occurring fine-tuning errors remains an open question.

Experimental Setup. We evaluate NormPre across model scales, architectures and datasets. Our experiments cover GPT-2 Small on OpenWebText ( Radford et al., 2019 ; Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019 ) , LLaMA-{130M, 350M, 1.3B} on C4 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Raffel et al., 2020 ) , and Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} on Pile ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2020 ) . We compare NormPre-G and NormPre-L with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and MANO ( Gu and Xie, 2026 ) . NormPre-G uses five Newton-Schulz iterations and NormPre-L uses the Sketch implementation with rank r = 32 r=32 . All models are trained for 10,000 10{,}000 steps with a sequence length of 1024 1024 and an effective batch size of 512 512 . Within each setting, all optimizers use matched model initialization, data order, training budget and evaluation protocol. Detailed configurations are provided in Appendix A.1 . Figure 1a shows training and validation loss trajectories averaged over three matched seeds. Both variants achieve lower training and validation loss than the baselines during later training, demonstrating the effectiveness of NormPre. Table 1 confirms that both variants outperform all three baselines in mean best validation loss, with NormPre-G achieving the lowest value. Compared with the strongest baseline Muon, NormPre-G and NormPre-L reduce validation loss by 0.0397 0.0397 and 0.0238 0.0238 , respectively.

LLaMA Pretraining on C4 and Qwen3 Pretraining on Pile. We extend the comparison to LLaMA-{130M, 350M, 1.3B} on C4 and Qwen3-{0.6B, 1.7B} on Pile. Table 1 and Figures 1b – 1d show that both variants consistently outperform all three baselines across these diverse architectures, with NormPre-G achieving the lowest loss. For LLaMA, the advantages over the strongest baseline are most pronounced at the largest evaluated scale (1.3B), where NormPre-G and NormPre-L reduce validation loss by 0.0392 0.0392 and 0.0301 0.0301 , respectively. These optimization gains extend similarly to Qwen3. Notably, NormPre-L performs closely to NormPre-G at the 1.7B scale with a minimal loss difference of 0.0029 0.0029 (Qwen3 loss curves are deferred to Appendix A.2 ).

Training Efficiency. Table 2 reports training efficiency on GPT-2 Small and LLaMA-1.3B under the same configurations as the main experiments. As summarized in Table 9 and Remark 1 (Appendix C ), NormPre-G shares Muon’s asymptotic complexity, but its additional normalization increases optimizer latency by 5.76 % 5.76\% and 4.37 % 4.37\% relative to Muon on the two models, respectively. NormPre-L approximates the interaction subspace via sketching, reducing optimizer latency by 38.12 % 38.12\% and 67.00 % 67.00\% . These optimizer-level differences have a smaller effect on end-to-end training efficiency because optimizer updates account for only a small fraction of step time, which is largely spent on forward and backward computation. Relative to Muon, NormPre-G increases step time by about 0.44 % 0.44\% and 0.08 % 0.08\% on both models, while NormPre-L reduces it by 1.16 % 1.16\% and 3.13 % 3.13\% , with corresponding improvements in throughput. Both variants remain slower per step than AdamW and MANO due to the additional spectral processing, but match the whole-training peak memory of Muon and MANO. Further discussions and efficiency results on Qwen3 are provided in Appendix A.2 .

Training and Validation Loss for Qwen3 Models. We provide the training and validation loss curves for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B on Pile in Figure 5 . For training loss, dark curves denote 50-step moving averages and light curves the raw trajectories. Training Efficiency Configurations. Efficiency measurements mirror the main pretraining configurations (including model architecture, sequence length of 1024, effective batch size of 512, and gradient clipping) with the following specific profiling protocols: • Precision & Data Loading: GPT-2 Small and LLaMA use FP32 parameters with BF16 autocast, while Qwen3 uses pure BF16. OpenWebText is fully materialized in host memory, whereas C4 and Pile are read dynamically from persistent NumPy memmaps (transferring only the active batch to the GPU to avoid full-dataset materialization). • Measurement Window: We profile 100 optimizer steps following 20 warmup steps. To isolate core algorithmic overhead, we disable optimizer diagnostics (e.g., descent alignment), validation, checkpointing, W&B logging, and torch.compile . • Metric Definitions: Optimizer latency isolates optimizer.step() using strict CUDA synchronization immediately before and after the call. E2E step time encompasses the complete training loop (data transfer, forward/backward passes, gradient accumulation, clipping, and optimizer update). Throughput is computed as global tokens per E2E step time, and peak memory tracks the maximum CUDA allocated memory during a measured step.
